citations.review_text:
Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number is a fantastic sequel and a worthy conclusion to one of the most memorable indie series of the 2010s.

It takes everything that made the first game so addictive and goes bigger: more characters, more weapons, more enemies, larger levels, more mechanics, and an even more ambitious story. The result is a longer and more varied experience that constantly pushes you to adapt your playstyle.

The different characters are a particularly interesting addition. Each one brings unique abilities or restrictions that completely change the way you approach an encounter, forcing you to rethink the fast and brutal gameplay you're used to. The game is at its best when it gives you the freedom to improvise, react to enemy behavior, and turn a chaotic situation into a perfectly executed massacre.

And, once again, the audiovisual presentation is incredible. The pixel art is more detailed, the animations are fantastic, and the soundtrack is absolutely phenomenal. With artists like Perturbator, Carpenter Brut, M|O|O|N and Jasper Byrne, the music is arguably one of the game's greatest strengths.

The story is also much more ambitious than the first game, following multiple characters and timelines as the consequences of the original game's events unfold. It can be confusing at times, but the atmosphere and presentation make it a fascinating conclusion to the saga.

Some levels are noticeably more open and gun-focused than in the first game, which can make certain encounters feel less fluid and more restrictive. But once you adapt to its design philosophy, there's an incredible amount of depth to discover.

And if the campaign isn't enough, the Hard Mode and level editor provide even more reasons to come back.

More ambitious, more brutal, more stylish, and absolutely unforgettable.

A fantastic sequel and a must-play for fans of the original.

Greatly expands on the world shown in the first Hotline Miami with a wide variety of characters. Soundtrack continues to be incredible, and lots of interesting new gameplay styles. However, I personally didn't like the level design at times.

If there was one word to describe this game it would definitely be "mindfck," and honestly thats exactly the feeling the writers were going for. I know the whole structure is meant to be pieced together, but going through it firsthand I didnt fully get why it needed to be this fragmented. You play as multiple characters throughout, hopping between perspectives and timelines, and it all just becomes too much to take in at once, to the point where you will most likely lose track of whats going on. For this game specifically, I see that as both a good and a bad thing. The good is that it genuinely puts you in this disoriented, numb headspace that mirrors exactly how the characters themselves feel, you dont know whats happening and youre desperately trying to piece it together as you push forward, chasing some kind of resolution. [spoiler] Except in the end there isnt really one, everyone and everything gets wiped out in a nuke, closing out this endless psychological war and killing spree the characters have been trapped in the whole time. [/spoiler] The bad, for me personally, is that they couldve told this with a cleaner, more straightforward timeline instead of constantly jumping back and forth. It just leaves the player feeling lost, to the point where you might give up trying to piece it together yourself and end up watching a video  explaining it all instead, which isnt really the experience you want. You want to be uncovering and understanding most of this firsthand. I do love going back afterward and connecting the dots, but if I couldve pieced together the main throughline while actually playing, this wouldve been a 10/10 for me easily. Its still a genuinely good game, but I kept getting caught up wondering how it ties back to the first one, over and over, until I finally looked into the explanation afterward and it clicked.
As for the gameplay, its a banger, same energy as the first game, maybe even better with how many characters there are and the variety in …

citations.review_text:
Some of the gameplay changes from Hotline Miami 1 are quite welcome (like the tighter gameplay focus, increased enemy variety and unique level attributes), but there are a whole host of new quality of life issues:
~ Some levels are unnecessarily dark for purely aesthetic reasons, making enemies hard to see.
~ The wide-open map design encourages enemies killing you from offscreen.
~ Doors are even jankier when interacting with enemy AI, made worse by slower executions that ruin your combo (which Hotline Miami is STILL heavily reliant on for their scoring system).
~ Baiting is still the dominant strategy for completing levels, which not only feels cheap but is also fickle due to inconsistent enemy visibility.
~ Ambitious as it is, it's hard to not think about how frustrating this game is compared to Hotline Miami 1, with a story that is deliberately alienating, confusing and self-contradicting.

claims.claim: Reviewers note that the game includes a workshop and a level editor for creating and playing custom maps.

citations.review_text:
Hotline Miami 2 feels like they wanted to tell an interesting story more than they cared to make a fun game. 
The open level design in combination with the dimwitted AI turns almost every encounter into the same scenario: discharge whatever firearm you're carrying and wait around the corner for the enemies to run into the meatgrinder. 
While this same argument could, in theory, also be levied against the first game, the lack of meaningful weapon variety and less responsive player controls (particularly, the small delay before you're able to pick up a dropped weapon, and the slower enemy executions) turn the original game's fast-paced sandbox charm into a fairly predictable and unstimulating slog.
The game does have its own merits, though, which are best seen in levels that experiment with different mission structure and provide exhilarating set-pieces. It's a shame Dennaton Games weren't interested in creating another sequel or spiritual successor, as Hotline Miami 2 feels like a perfect experiment that precedes a subsequent game which ties it all together and brings along the best parts of both.
As its own game it is definitely worth one full playthrough. But I do think that it is a starkly different experience when compared to the original, and, due to that, suffers from not being able to fit the expectations born from playing the first.
P.S. Most of my playtime thereafter had been spent playing in the Mario-Maker like level editor, where you can take whatever criticisms you have against the game's level design and try to remedy them yourselves. And I admit - it does improve the experience by a lot; and there are also a great amount of  perfect levels and campaigns made by the community available on the Steam Workshop. That being said, I still feel more compelled to boot up the original Hotline Miami, as opposed to Hotline 2, whenever I feel like playing a top-down shooter. This is why it doesn't really feel right to me to recommend it.

citations.review_text:
Hotline Miami 2 feels like they wanted to tell an interesting story more than they cared to make a fun game. 
The open level design in combination with the dimwitted AI turns almost every encounter into the same scenario: discharge whatever firearm you're carrying and wait around the corner for the enemies to run into the meatgrinder. 
While this same argument could, in theory, also be levied against the first game, the lack of meaningful weapon variety and less responsive player controls (particularly, the small delay before you're able to pick up a dropped weapon, and the slower enemy executions) turn the original game's fast-paced sandbox charm into a fairly predictable and unstimulating slog.
The game does have its own merits, though, which are best seen in levels that experiment with different mission structure and provide exhilarating set-pieces. It's a shame Dennaton Games weren't interested in creating another sequel or spiritual successor, as Hotline Miami 2 feels like a perfect experiment that precedes a subsequent game which ties it all together and brings along the best parts of both.
As its own game it is definitely worth one full playthrough. But I do think that it is a starkly different experience when compared to the original, and, due to that, suffers from not being able to fit the expectations born from playing the first.
P.S. Most of my playtime thereafter had been spent playing in the Mario-Maker like level editor, where you can take whatever criticisms you have against the game's level design and try to remedy them yourselves. And I admit - it does improve the experience by a lot; and there are also a great amount of  perfect levels and campaigns made by the community available on the Steam Workshop. That being said, I still feel more compelled to boot up the original Hotline Miami, as opposed to Hotline 2, whenever I feel like playing a top-down shooter. This is why it doesn't really feel right to me to recommend it.

Masterpiece.

100000000/10

Best soundtrack in a game OAT. (It's not a OST however)

The gameplay is awesome for me, but I definitely see how it misses for some.

However the story, characters, and writing, mixed with the important messaging that the developers were trying to convey, make this a true classic and must play in my opinion. This is a forever top 5 game for me, and whether you're someone just chasing a rush, or looking for something so much deeper, you'll find it in this game.

[i]Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number[/i] is a very interesting case. 

The original hypnotic video game was a commentary on violence and our acceptance of it. The sequel is not without its missteps however; the actual gameplay can be significantly more frustrating due to bad level design resulting in getting killed from enemies off screen, and a significant increase in playstyle restrictions. The specific playstyles the game allows you to experience can be very fun, but then you'll be stuck in a level where you're forced to engage in equally unfun playstyles (most notably the jungle levels). 

The narrative itself is nonlinear and told intentionally out of order, meant to elicit specific understandings to form an emotional arc that makes sense even if the plot will be unclear. The game will reveal plot points in the style of an arthouse movie, but you will only really start to understand the overall story over the course of additional playthroughs.

Despite all these ambitions, I think Dennaton essentially accomplished the same result using less with the original [i]Hotline Miami[i/]. While an interesting experiment, the multiple errors make the sequel fail to reach the heights of the original game. I would still recommend fans of the original to play the sequel with all this in mind though.
